title: Spot and Avoid Medicare Open Enrollment Scams

sections.text: Why Medicare Open Enrollment Attracts Scammers

sections.content: Every year between October 15 and December 7, millions of Medicare beneficiaries review their coverage and consider switching plans. Scammers know this window well, and they use it to their advantage by impersonating Medicare, plan carriers, or licensed agents to appear trustworthy. Because many older adults may be less familiar with digital verification tools or newer scam tactics, they are frequently targeted during this period.

Recognizing this seasonal pattern does not mean you need to treat every phone call or email with suspicion. It simply means knowing what to watch for so you can make enrollment decisions with confidence instead of worry.

sections.text: Red Flags in Phone Calls Claiming to Be From Medicare

sections.content: Medicare will never call you out of the blue to ask for your Medicare number, Social Security number, or banking information. If you receive a call like this, that alone is a sign something is wrong. Legitimate licensed agents only call you if you requested information, filled out a form, or otherwise gave prior consent to be contacted.

Be cautious of callers who pressure you to decide immediately or who threaten that your coverage will be cancelled if you do not act right away. Scammers rely on urgency to prevent you from pausing to verify who they really are. It also helps to know that caller ID can be spoofed, so a call that appears to come from a government number is not proof that it actually is one.

sections.text: Phrases Scammers Use to Sound Official

items: Claims that you have a "new Medicare card" and need to verify your information to receive it
Mentions of limited-time plan upgrades or rebates tied to your Social Security number
Urgent language such as "your benefits will be cancelled today" if you do not respond immediately

sections.calloutText: Medicare does not call, text, or email you unexpectedly to ask for personal or banking details. Any contact that does this, no matter how official it sounds, should be treated as a red flag.

sections.text: Red Flags in Text Messages and Emails

sections.content: Unsolicited text messages or emails asking you to "confirm" your Medicare details through a link are almost always fraudulent. Legitimate Medicare communications will not ask you to click a shortened or unfamiliar link to verify personal information.

Look closely at the sender's name and email address. Scam messages often include misspellings, odd domain names, or generic greetings like "Dear Member" instead of your actual name. Avoid clicking links or downloading attachments from any unexpected Medicare-related message, even if it looks convincing.

If you want to check something related to your coverage, go directly to a trusted source such as [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/) or the verified website of your plan carrier rather than following a link sent to you.

sections.text: Common Medicare Scam Tactics During Enrollment Season

sections.content: Scammers use several recurring tactics each fall, and recognizing them can help you avoid becoming a target. Some offer "free" genetic testing, braces, or medical equipment as a way to collect your Medicare number for fraudulent billing. Others show up at your door or call unsolicited, offering to "help" you enroll in a plan on the spot.

items: Imposters posing as licensed agents who ask for payment before your enrollment is actually complete
Door-to-door visits or unsolicited calls pressuring an immediate plan switch
Scammers referencing real plan names, carriers, or enrollment dates to sound credible

sections.content: No legitimate plan enrollment requires upfront payment to a person claiming to be an agent, and no real agent needs to visit your home without your invitation.

sections.text: How to Protect Your Personal Information While Comparing Plans

sections.content: Treat your Medicare number with the same level of privacy as your Social Security number. Share it only with sources you have personally verified, such as your doctor's office, pharmacy, or a licensed agent you contacted directly.

Before sharing any details with someone claiming to be a licensed Medicare agent, you can verify their license through your state insurance department. When comparing plans, rely on official sources like Medicare.gov or a transparent, verified helpline rather than information from an unsolicited call or ad.

Take your time when comparing coverage options. No legitimate source of help will require you to make a decision on the spot, and a transparent agent will welcome your questions rather than rush you past them.

Before you share any Medicare or personal details with someone offering help, ask directly: "Are you a licensed agent, and can you confirm your license number so I can verify it?" A legitimate agent will answer without hesitation, while a scammer will often change the subject or apply pressure instead.

sections.text: What to Do If You Suspect a Scam

sections.content: If something about a call, text, or email feels off, stop responding right away. Hang up the phone or close the message without confirming any personal details, even if the caller pushes back or asks you to stay on the line.

items: Report suspicious activity to the Medicare fraud line at 1-800-MEDICARE or contact your state's Senior Medicare Patrol (SMP)
File a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov if you shared money or personal information
Review your Medicare Summary Notices regularly for unfamiliar charges or services you do not recognize

sections.content: Acting quickly after a suspected scam can limit the damage and help investigators flag the activity for other beneficiaries. The [Senior Medicare Patrol program](https://www.ssa.gov/) and your Medicare account are both useful resources for catching unfamiliar billing early.

sections.text: How to Get Trustworthy Help Without the Pressure

sections.content: A licensed Medicare agent should explain your options clearly, answer your questions directly, and never rush you toward a decision. Trustworthy resources are transparent about which plans are available in your area, how their licensing works, and how the help they offer is actually provided.

Signs of a reliable resource include plain-language explanations, visible reviews from real clients, and a willingness to let you set the pace. You should feel free to ask questions and compare coverage, costs, doctors, and prescriptions for as long as you need before committing to anything.

faqs.question: I'm worried about scams, so how do I know it's safe to talk to someone about my Medicare options?
faqs.answer: Verify the agent's license through your state insurance department before sharing any personal details. A reputable agent will be transparent about their licensing and will not ask for your Medicare number, Social Security number, or payment information upfront. If someone pressures you before you've confirmed who they are, treat that as a warning sign.

faqs.question: How can I compare Medicare plans without getting a pushy sales call?
faqs.answer: Start with official tools like Medicare.gov's Plan Finder, and if you contact an agent, ask upfront how often they'll follow up and whether you can set the pace. Trustworthy resources let you control the timeline and won't flood you with repeated calls or emails.

faqs.question: Can I research Medicare on my own before deciding who to trust for help?
faqs.answer: Yes, reviewing Medicare.gov and other verified materials on your own is a good first step. Understanding the basics ahead of time, such as plan types and enrollment deadlines, often makes later conversations with a licensed agent faster and more productive.

faqs.question: What if I already shared personal information with someone I now think was a scammer?
faqs.answer: Contact 1-800-MEDICARE and your state's Senior Medicare Patrol right away, and consider alerting the major credit bureaus if financial information was shared. Acting quickly limits potential damage, and this is a manageable, fairly common situation that fraud reporting channels are built to handle.

sections.text: Stay Informed and Protect Your Coverage

sections.content: Protecting your Medicare coverage during open enrollment starts with verifying who you're talking to before sharing any personal details. Whenever possible, review plan options directly through Medicare.gov or a transparent, licensed resource rather than responding to unsolicited calls or messages.
If you're ready to compare your Medicare options, you can reach out to a licensed resource for guidance that lets you ask questions and move at your own pace, without pressure to decide on the spot.
